one_line: Braintrust workshop on AI observability: trace agents, score production traffic with judges and topics, and let a coding agent run the eval-and-fix flywheel through the Braintrust CLI.
summary: Doug Guthrie, a solutions engineer at Braintrust, runs a hands-on workshop on turning agent traces into quality signal. He argues that tracing is the foundation, that production data should feed back into development in a loop, and that scores (code-based, LLM judge, and human-calibrated judge) make that loop measurable. The talk introduces Topics, which clusters production traces into patterns to find failure modes nobody wrote a test for, and walks through setting up tracing, offline evals, online scorers, automations and a custom facet on a demo support agent. The second half shows a coding agent (Codex) using the Braintrust CLI and SQL to find failure clusters, add examples to a dataset, and propose agent changes, with a GitHub Action sketch that opens PRs. Most of the content is practical, but the talk is also a product pitch, and several competitive and cost claims are vendor assertions without shown evidence.

key_ideas.idea: Tracing is the foundation of agent observability
key_ideas.detail: Without a trace of every step, its inputs and outputs, the agent is a black box and quality regressions cannot be located. Capture everything first, then derive signal.

key_ideas.idea: Production should inform development through a repeatable flywheel
key_ideas.detail: Loop: observe production, derive insight at scale, change the agent, run an eval to check for regression, then deploy. The speaker says the loop should be easy enough that most teams can plug it in.

key_ideas.idea: Signal comes in three kinds of scores
key_ideas.detail: Code-based checks (schema validity, tool call order) are fast and cheap. LLM judges handle subjective criteria. A third kind is an LLM judge whose output is checked against human review. A code-based score can also call an LLM for branching logic.

key_ideas.idea: Judges need calibration, and harsh tests matter
key_ideas.detail: Human review of judge output should be an ongoing practice, since agents and scores both change. Binary pass/fail is preferred over graded scales early on. If every eval passes, the test cases or scores are probably too easy.

key_ideas.idea: Offline evals and online scoring answer different questions
key_ideas.detail: Offline evals (run in CI on a dataset) answer whether a change regressed. Online scorers run on live traffic as it arrives and show where production is failing.

key_ideas.idea: Topics find unknown unknowns that fixed scores miss
key_ideas.detail: Known failure modes are already covered by eval scores. Topics clusters production traces so that unexpected user intents, sentiments and issues surface, including feature requests and silent failures.

key_ideas.idea: Topics pipeline: preprocess, facet, summarize, embed, cluster
key_ideas.detail: A default preprocessor reduces a large trace to user, assistant and tool turns. A facet (task, issues, sentiment, or a custom prompt) summarizes it. The summary is embedded and clustered into a topic map that labels traces. Custom preprocessors and facets can be supplied.

key_ideas.idea: Use an LLM-written issue facet with an exclusion regex to keep only real problems
key_ideas.detail: The custom facet prompt tells the model to output a none value when nothing is wrong, and a regex drops those outputs so the topic map shows only failures. A facet that never reaches the minimum match count simply produces no topic.

key_ideas.idea: Production traces should flow back into the eval dataset
key_ideas.detail: Curate edge-case traces from production into the dataset, add a score for the newly seen failure, then rerun the eval and compare to the last run. The speaker frames evals as a baseline that must evolve with the agent.

key_ideas.idea: A coding agent can run the whole flywheel through the CLI and SQL
key_ideas.detail: With the Braintrust CLI and agent skills, Codex queries traces with SQL, finds failure clusters, inspects example traces, adds dataset rows, and proposes code changes. The speaker says this can run in a GitHub Action that opens PRs for human review, and that a customer produces 5 to 10 extra PRs a day this way.

techniques.name: Binary, harsh LLM judges with examples in the prompt
techniques.how: Use pass/fail criteria instead of A-to-D grades, include few-shot examples in the judge prompt, and use a stronger model for judging than for generation. Ask the judge to return its reasoning so humans can audit it.
techniques.when: When first putting an agent into production or when all evals are passing and the test set may be too easy.

techniques.name: Human-calibrated judges
techniques.how: Add a review interface where users or reviewers grade judged outputs, then compare judge scores to those labels and adjust the judge prompt.
techniques.when: Whenever judge outputs drive decisions on live traffic, and especially for online scoring.

techniques.name: Scores defined in code and pushed to the platform
techniques.how: Keep scorers in the repo (for example with a make push-scorers target) and push them to the platform so they are version controlled and reusable in the playground. Code-based scorers can bundle their dependencies on push, so they don't need a separate async service.
techniques.when: When scorers have complex dependencies, or you want them under version control and shared with non-engineers.

techniques.name: Automation rules with scope and sampling for online scoring
techniques.how: Attach scorers to new logs with a rule. Choose the scope: trace, span (with a filter such as span name), or group (for multi-turn chats, grouped by a conversation ID). Set a sampling rate, starting high for a new agent and lowering it as the agent matures.
techniques.when: When you need to score live traffic and control cost. Use group scope when a conversation spans several traces.

techniques.name: Topic windows and filters for long conversations
techniques.how: Configure the topic window (for example one or two days) and filters so the pipeline sees the conversation history it needs, and run topic jobs only on matching traces.
techniques.when: When user sessions last much longer than a single trace and clustering needs context across turns.

techniques.name: Coding agent as flywheel operator
techniques.how: Give a coding agent the CLI and skills to write SQL over traces and spans, read scores and topics, create dataset rows, run evals, and propose code changes. The output is a PR with SQL queries, aggregate results and links to experiments, and a human reviews it.
techniques.when: When production traces are too large to review by hand, and you want an automated loop that stays auditable.

techniques.name: Service account for the analysis loop
techniques.how: Lock the raw-trace project so engineers cannot read it. Run the automated analysis under a service account that has access, and share aggregated results and queries with the team instead of raw user data.
techniques.when: When trace data contains sensitive user content and you still want insights and PRs produced from it.

techniques.name: Remote eval exposed to a playground
techniques.how: Wrap an eval task with declared parameters (for example system prompt and model) and serve it from your own infrastructure. A playground then calls the endpoint so product or domain users can edit prompts and run evals without touching the code.
techniques.when: When PMs or subject-matter experts should iterate on prompts or tool descriptions without an engineer in the loop.

techniques.name: Mutable spans for attaching scores later
techniques.how: Update existing spans in place to attach scores, metadata or metrics, using the span ID, so scoring can run as a separate process after the fact.
techniques.when: When scores are produced asynchronously or by a separate service after the trace was logged.

numbers.claim: Topics pipeline price: $0.06 per million input tokens and $0.48 per million output tokens (speaker says it is cheaper than an LLM judge at 100% of traces)
Topics needs at least 100 facet matches before a topic appears; the speaker's issues facet had fewer, so no issues topic was produced
Workshop import: 968 traces and 5,260 spans loaded via BT Sync (speaker first said 1,052 spans, then corrected to 5,260)
One large customer generates 5 to 10 extra PRs per day with the automated flywheel
The speaker estimates about 90% of the large customers shown on the logo slide run a self-hosted data plane
Braintrust built its own backend (Brainstore) in late 2024 after ClickHouse fell down at scale for its largest customers
Braintrust CLI released in late February, with a user conference that year
Judge sampling rate: new agents run high sampling, scaled back as the agent matures and the scores stop finding new problems

hot_takes: Observability is shifting from passive dashboards to 'active observability' that hands back insights, not raw data (vendor framing).
If every eval passes, the test cases or scores are too easy, not the agent good.
Using the platform's hosted topics model can be cheaper than an LLM judge at 100% of traces (the speaker's cost claim is not shown with data).
Braintrust's own database is said to be about a year ahead of competitors (vendor claim).
LLM judges should always be checked against human review, and judges are not set and forget.
The speaker says customers would rather keep a custom-built ClickHouse or self-built store than the vendor's off-the-shelf storage, which is a sales claim, not a measured result.

relevance.why: AgentOS already plans trace-driven skill mining (SkillForge) and a telemetry layer. The talk's topics pipeline and online scorers are a concrete pattern for turning that telemetry into labelled failure clusters.
relevance.action: Prototype a cheap clustering facet over AgentOS proxy traces (summarize, embed, cluster) and compare its cost per trace to an LLM judge on the same sample before building the SkillForge success signal.

relevance.why: ProsHarness runs loops and schedules around Claude Code. The talk shows a scheduled coding-agent job that reads traces and scores, proposes changes, and opens a PR. It also shows a service-account pattern to keep raw traces locked down.
relevance.action: Add a ProsHarness scheduled job that reads online eval scores and failure clusters, proposes an agent change as a PR with query evidence, and keeps the raw traces behind a service account.
